label: Sayings CXXXVI–CLVII
paragraphs: CXXXVI. That man is free who lives as he wishes, who cannot be compelled or hindered or forced, whose impulses are unimpeded, whose desires reach their goal, whose aversions do not fall into what they would avoid. Who, then, wants to live in error? "No one." Who wants to live deceived, rash, unjust, undisciplined, complaining of his lot, mean? "No one." So no bad man lives as he wishes; and so he is not free either.

CXXXVII. This is what the more cautious travelers do too. A man has heard that the road is infested with robbers. He does not dare set out alone; he waits for the company of an ambassador, or a quaestor, or a proconsul, attaches himself to it, and passes through safely. The wise man does the same in the universe. "There are many bands of robbers, tyrants, storms, hardships, losses of what is dearest. Where is a man to take refuge? How is he to pass through without being robbed? What company is he to wait for, to get through safely? To whom is he to attach himself? To so-and-so, the rich man, the man of consular rank? And what good is that to me? He is stripped himself; he wails; he mourns. And what if my fellow traveler himself turns on me and becomes my robber? What shall I do? I will be a friend of Caesar. No one will wrong me if I am his companion. But first, to become one, how much I must endure and suffer, how often and by how many I must be robbed! And then, if I do become one, he too is mortal. And if by some turn of events he becomes my enemy, where is it best for me to withdraw to? To the wilderness? Come, does fever not go there? What then is to be done? Is it not possible to find a fellow traveler who is safe, trustworthy, strong, proof against plots?" So he reflects, and comes to see that if he attaches himself to God, he will pass through safely.

CXXXVIII. "What do you mean by attaching himself?" That whatever God wills, he wills too, and whatever God does not will, he does not will either. "How can that be done?" How else than by studying God's impulses and his governance?

CXXXIX. Then, when you have received everything from another, even your own self, are you indignant, and do you blame the giver if he takes something away from you? Who are you, and what did you come here for? Was it not he who brought you in? Was it not he who showed you the light? Has he not given you fellow workers? And senses too? And reason? And as what did he bring you in? Was it not as a mortal? Was it not as one who would live on the earth with a little bit of flesh, and watch his governance, and join in his procession and keep festival with him for a short time? Will you not, then, after watching the procession and the festival for as long as it is given you, go when he leads you out, bowing down to him and giving thanks for what you have heard and seen? "No; I wanted to go on keeping the festival." Yes, and the initiates want to go on being initiated, and perhaps the people at Olympia want to see more athletes. But the festival has an end. Leave; go away grateful and self-respecting. Make room for others. Others too must be born, as you were born.

CXL. Why are you insatiable? Why are you never satisfied? Why do you crowd the universe? "Yes, but I want my little children with me, and my wife." Are they yours, then? Do they not belong to the one who gave them, the one who also made you? Will you not give up what is another's? Will you not give way to the one who is stronger? "Then why did he bring me in on these terms?" If it does not suit you, leave. He has no need of a spectator who complains of his lot. He needs those who will join in the festival and the dance, so that they may applaud all the more, and be filled with awe, and sing hymns to the festival. But those who cannot bear hardship, and the cowards, he will not be sorry to see left out of the festival. For when they were here they did not behave as at a feast, or fill the place that suited them. They were in pain, and they blamed their guardian divinity, their fortune, their companions; they had no sense of what they had been given, or of their own powers, which they received for the very opposite: greatness of soul, nobility, courage, and this freedom we are now inquiring about.

CXLI. "And you," someone says, "are you free?" By the gods, I wish to be and I pray to be, but I cannot yet look my masters in the face. I still set value on this poor body; I care a great deal about keeping it whole, though it is not whole as it is. But I can show you a free man, so that you need not go on looking for an example. Diogenes was free. How so? Not because he was born of free parents, for he was not, but because he himself was free, because he had thrown off every handle by which slavery could take hold, and there was no way anyone could get near him, nothing by which anyone could seize him to make him a slave. Everything he had was easily untied; everything was only fastened on. If you had taken hold of his property, he would have let it go to you rather than follow you for its sake; if of his leg, his leg; if of his whole poor body, his whole poor body; and the same with family, friends, and country. He knew where he had them from, and from whom, and on what terms. But his true ancestors, the gods, and his real country he would never have abandoned, nor would he have let anyone outdo him in obeying them and submitting to them, and no one would have died for his country more cheerfully. For he never tried to seem to be doing anything for the sake of the whole; he remembered that everything that happens comes from there, and is done for the sake of that country, and is ordered by the one who governs it.

CXLII. Study these things, these judgments, these arguments; look to these examples, if you want to be free, if you desire the thing as it deserves. And what wonder is it if you buy so great a thing at so great a price? For the sake of what is commonly thought freedom some men hang themselves, others throw themselves from cliffs, and whole cities have at times been destroyed. For the sake of the true freedom, which cannot be plotted against and is secure, will you not give back to God, when he asks for it, what he gave? Will you not practice, as Plato says, not only dying but being tortured and exiled and flogged; in a word, giving back everything that is not your own? Otherwise you will be a slave among slaves, even if you are consul ten thousand times, even if you go up to the Palace; no less a slave. And you will find that what the philosophers say may perhaps be contrary to opinion, as Cleanthes used to say, but it is not contrary to reason.
CXLIII. Asked how a man could best grieve his enemy, Epictetus said, "By setting himself to live the best life he can."

CXLIV. For I am free and a friend of God, so as to obey him willingly. I must lay claim to nothing else: not body, not property, not office, not reputation; in a word, nothing. For he does not want me to lay claim to them. If he had wanted that, he would have made them good for me. But as it is he has not; so I cannot break any of his commands. Guard your own good in everything; as for the rest, take what is given, so far as to act reasonably in it, and be content with that alone. Otherwise you will be unfortunate, you will be unhappy, you will be hindered, you will be impeded. These are the laws sent from there, these are the decrees. A man should become an interpreter of these, and subject to these, not to those of Masurius and Cassius.

CXLV. Remember that it is not only the desire for office and wealth that makes men mean and subject to others, but also the desire for quiet, and leisure, and travel, and learning. In a word, whatever the external thing is, to set a value on it makes you subject to another. What difference is there, then, between desiring a seat in the senate and desiring not to be a senator? What difference between desiring office and desiring to be out of office? What difference between saying, "I am in a bad way, I have nothing to do, I am tied to my books like a corpse," and saying, "I am in a bad way, I have no leisure to read"? For just as greetings and office are among the external things, outside the will, so is a book. Or why do you want to read? Tell me. If you stop at the reading itself, to be entertained or to learn something, you are a shallow and miserable fellow. But if you refer it to what you should, what is that but a life that flows smoothly? And if reading does not win you a life that flows smoothly, what use is it? "But it does," he says, "and that is why I am upset at being cut off from it." And what kind of smooth flow is this, which anyone who comes along can impede; I do not say Caesar or Caesar's friend, but a raven, a flute player, a fever, thirty thousand other things? Nothing so marks a life that flows smoothly as that it is unbroken and unimpeded.

CXLVI. If you have put away ill nature and abuse, or made them less; if you have put away rashness, foul language, carelessness, slackness; if you are not moved by the things that moved you before, or at least not in the same way as before, then you can keep a festival every day: today because you behaved well in this matter, tomorrow because you behaved well in another. How much greater a reason for sacrifice than a consulship or a governorship!

CXLVII. These things come to you from yourself and from the gods. Remember who the giver is, and to whom he gives, and for what. Brought up on reasonings like these, do you still care where you will be happy, where you will please God? Are the gods not equally distant from every place? Do they not see what happens equally from everywhere?

CXLVIII. For this has been given by God to each man unhindered. These judgments make for affection in a household, concord in a city, peace among nations; they make a man grateful to God and confident everywhere, since he is dealing with things that are another's, things of no worth.
CXLIX. If you are seeking the truth, you will not seek to win by every means; and when you have found the truth, you will have this, that you cannot be beaten.
CL. And what nonsense is this? How do I still hold right judgments if I am not content to be what I am, but am in a flutter about what I seem to be?

CLI. God has made everything in the universe, and the universe itself as a whole, unhindered and complete in itself, and the parts of it for the use of the whole. Now all other creatures have been left without the power to understand his governance; but the rational creature has the means to reason out all these things: that it is a part, and what kind of part, and that it is right for the parts to give way to the whole. Besides this, being by nature noble, great of soul, and free, it sees that of the things around it some are unhindered and in its own power, and others are hindered and in the power of others: unhindered, what lies within the will; hindered, what lies outside the will. And so, if it thinks its own good and advantage lie only in these, in the things that are unhindered and in its own power, it will be free, its life will flow smoothly, it will be happy, unharmed, great-minded, pious, grateful to God for everything, never finding fault with anything that happens, never accusing anyone. But if it thinks they lie in external things outside the will, it must be hindered and impeded, and be a slave to those who have power over the things it admires and fears; it must be impious, since it thinks God is harming it, and unfair, always trying to get more for itself; and it must be mean and petty.

CLII. Whom, then, can I still fear? The men who guard the bedchamber? Fear that they will do what? Shut me out? If they find me wanting to go in, let them shut me out. "Then why do you come to the door?" Because I think it my duty, as long as the game goes on, to join in the game. "How is it, then, that you are not shut out?" Because if no one lets me in, I do not want to go in; I always want what happens instead. For I think what God wills is better than what I will. I will attach myself to him as a servant and follower; I share his impulse, I share his desire; in a word, I share his will. There is no shutting out for me, only for those who try to force their way in.
CLIII. But what does Socrates say? "Just as one man rejoices in improving his farm," he says, "and another his horse, so I rejoice day by day in watching myself grow better."

CLIV. The dress is fitted to the craft, but men take their name from the craft, not from the dress. That is why Euphrates was right to say, "For a long time I tried to keep it hidden that I was a philosopher, and this was useful to me. For first, I knew that whatever I did well I did not for the spectators but for myself. I ate properly, for myself; I kept my look and my walk composed; all for myself and for God. Then, as I competed alone, so I alone ran the risk. If I did anything shameful or unbecoming, the cause of philosophy was not put at risk, and I did not harm the many by going wrong as a philosopher. So those who did not know my aim wondered how it was that, though I kept company with all the philosophers and lived with them, I was not a philosopher myself. And what harm was there in having the philosopher recognized by what I did, and not by the badges?"

CLV. Practice first not being known for what you are; be a philosopher for yourself for a little while. That is how fruit comes. The seed must be buried for a time, and hidden, and grow little by little, so that it may come to full growth. But if it puts out the ear before the stalk has a joint, it is imperfect, a plant from a garden of Adonis. You are a little plant of that kind too. You have flowered sooner than you should, and the winter will scorch you.

CLVI. First, condemn what you are doing; then, when you have condemned it, do not despair of yourself, and do not be like those mean-spirited people who, once they have given in, surrender completely and are swept away as if by a current. Learn instead from the wrestling masters. The boy has fallen. "Get up," the master says, "and wrestle again, until you have made yourself strong." Be like that yourself. For know that nothing is easier to lead than the human soul. You have only to will it, and it is done; it is set right. And again, you have only to doze off, and it is lost. For both ruin and rescue come from within.

CLVII. It is difficulties that show what men are. So when a difficulty comes, remember that God, like a trainer, has matched you with a rough young man. "What for?" someone says. So that you may become an Olympic victor; and that does not happen without sweat.

divergences.phrase: ὅτι ὁ θεὸς πάντα πεποίηκεν τὰ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ
divergences.older: "God hath made all things in the world" (Crossley, as an opening statement)
divergences.lectio: "God has made everything in the universe"
divergences.note: In Arrian this is the second half of a question: "A man can be brought to this state by madness, and the Galileans by habit; can no one learn by reason and proof that God has made everything …?" Crossley began after the question mark's first half and dropped the Galileans, the one mention of Christians in Epictetus. The half he kept stands by itself, so Lectio keeps his extent and records the cut here. The "rational creature" (τὸ λογικὸν ζῷον) is neuter in Greek and "it" in the English.

divergences.phrase: παράδοξα μὲν ἴσως φασὶν οἱ φιλόσοφοι … οὐ μὴν παράλογα
divergences.older: "though the words of philosophers may run counter to the opinions of the world, yet have they reason on their side" (Crossley)
divergences.lectio: "what the philosophers say may perhaps be contrary to opinion … but it is not contrary to reason"
divergences.note: Cleanthes' saying turns on two words built alike, paradoxa and paraloga. English can carry the pair with "contrary to opinion" and "contrary to reason", so the Greek words are not named (Meditations policy 7).

divergences.lectio: Crossley's saying put into current English
divergences.note: A fragment from the late anthologies in Schweighäuser's collection; Schenkl does not print it and no Greek was to hand (it is Schweighäuser's fragment 130). The only paragraph in this section made from Crossley's English, checked against George Long's independent version (1877): "By preparing himself to live the best life that he can." It needs the Greek before the edition is called ready.
